Alexander Pope's translation of Homer's Iliad, published between seventeen fifteen and seventeen twenty, is an English verse rendering in heroic couplets that became the standard English Homer for over a century. Though not a literal translation, Pope's elegant, energetic couplets achieved a marriage of Augustan wit and classical grandeur that made Homer speak fluently in eighteenth-century English.

Pope published the work in six volumes over five years. It was an immediate commercial and critical success that made Pope's fortune and established him as England's preeminent poet. He rendered it in rhymed heroic couplets with strict symmetry and closure, with every couplet a unit of meaning, quite unlike the dactylic hexameter of Greek but perfectly suited to the neoclassical taste. Pope added hundreds of prefatory and marginal notes, scholarly apparatus that positioned him as both poet and critic, defending Homer against charges of imperfection.

His translation is famously improved Homer. He rounded rough speeches into elegant arguments, added symmetry and wit Homer lacked, and softened brutality, making gods more refined. Contemporary critics praised the fluency and noted the deviations, though by the nineteenth century scholars recognized Pope had translated Homer into Pope, not Homer into English. The companion Odyssey, published between seventeen twenty-five and seventeen twenty-six with William Broome and Elijah Fenton, was less wholly Pope's but equally polished. Together they gave English readers a complete Homeric text. Pope's version was superseded in the nineteenth century by more literal translations, though Pope's couplets remain the most quotable English Homer for certain passages.
